purpose: A technique-and-doneness protocol for home bakers that selects the correct mixing method for a target crumb, controls the thermal windows of fat, yeast, chocolate, and egg, drives fermentation and proof to measurable endpoints, judges doneness by an explicit signal hierarchy in which internal temperature dominates, accounts for carryover and cool-set, and diagnoses failures by differential signals so lookalike defects with opposite fixes are never treated the same way.
assumptions: no observed dataset supplied; all scores are heuristic priors
temperatures are stated in Celsius with the practical home-oven and instant-read-thermometer context in mind
the reader has a calibrated instant-read probe thermometer and a way to control dough and ingredient temperature
recipes referenced are conventional wheat-flour and egg-based baking unless a node names an exception (gluten-free, wild yeast)
ingredient ratios and formulation are assumed correct; this KB governs technique and doneness, not recipe balance
exclusions: recipe formulation and ingredient-ratio balancing (flour/sugar/fat/liquid proportions) — a formulation KB owns that
food-safety pathogen kill-step temperatures for meat and poultry; doneness here is about structure and set, not sanitization
flavor development chemistry (Maillard/caramelization palate tuning) beyond its role as a doneness color cue
equipment purchasing advice and oven-brand specifics beyond calibration and convection behavior
decorating, plating, and finishing techniques after the item is baked and set

competency_questions.question: How do you decide which technique to use and, in principle, how do you know when something is done rather than guessing?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: TECHNIQUE_DONENESS_FRAMEWORK states that method is chosen by target crumb and that doneness is measured against a signal hierarchy; DONENESS_SIGNAL_HIERARCHY names internal temperature as the dominant signal

competency_questions.question: Which mixing method produces which crumb, and how do you pick one for a given product?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MIXING_METHOD_SELECTION maps creaming, muffin/two-bowl, biscuit/cut-in, and foam/sponge to their resulting textures and selection criteria

competency_questions.question: What is the creaming method's mechanism and the fat temperature window it requires?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CREAMING_METHOD states the ~18-21°C plasticity window and explains aeration by fat trapping air around sugar crystals

competency_questions.question: How do the muffin/two-bowl and biscuit/cut-in methods differ, and what texture does each protect?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: MUFFIN_TWO_BOWL_METHOD and BISCUIT_CUT_IN_METHOD each state their fat state, mixing limit, and resulting crumb (tender quick-bread vs flaky layered)

competency_questions.question: What are the egg-foam whip stages and how do you fold to preserve the air?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FOAM_SPONGE_METHOD names soft/medium/stiff peak stages and FOLDING_PROTOCOL gives the cut-and-turn technique that avoids deflation

competency_questions.question: How is gluten developed and tested, and how does lamination depend on it?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: GLUTEN_DEVELOPMENT_KNEADING describes kneading to the windowpane endpoint and LAMINATION_BASICS states the cool butter window (~13-16°C) that keeps layers distinct

competency_questions.question: What are the yeast temperature bands for rehydration, dough target, stress, and death, and how do ADY and instant differ?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: YEAST_TEMPERATURE_BANDS states ADY rehydrate 40-43°C, instant direct-add with dough target 24-27°C, stress ~46°C, and death 54-60°C

competency_questions.question: How do you tell when fermentation and proof are at their endpoints, and what happens during oven spring?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: FERMENTATION_PROOF_ENDPOINTS gives the poke test and volume-fraction endpoints and OVEN_SPRING explains the final rapid rise before set

competency_questions.question: How do you temper chocolate and how do you temper eggs, and why are both called tempering?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: CHOCOLATE_TEMPERING states dark ~31-32°C and milk/white ~29-30°C working targets and EGG_TEMPERING describes gradual heat equalization to avoid curdling

competency_questions.question: What internal temperatures signal doneness for each product family, and why does temperature dominate the other cues?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: INTERNAL_TEMP_TARGETS lists lean bread 96-99°C, enriched lower, butter/sponge cakes 93-99°C, cheesecake 65-70°C, molten 71-77°C, custard 76-82°C, and DONENESS_SIGNAL_HIERARCHY asserts temperature's dominance

competency_questions.question: What secondary doneness cues exist and how do carryover and cool-set change when you should pull an item?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SECONDARY_DONENESS_CUES ranks skewer, springback, and color below temperature; CARRYOVER_COOL_SET explains pulling early to land on target after residual rise and set

competency_questions.question: How do you diagnose sunk centers, dense crumb, tough crumb, and tunneling by differential signals, and how do you decide recovery versus prevention?
competency_questions.acceptance_condition: SUNKEN_CENTER_DIAGNOSIS distinguishes wet-skewer from dry-crater sinks with opposite fixes, DENSE_CRUMB_DIAGNOSIS and TOUGH_CRUMB_TUNNELING separate their lookalike causes, and RECOVERY_VS_PREVENTION states what is salvageable versus preventable

glossary.definition: The temperature band (~18-21°C for butter) in which fat is firm enough to hold and stretch around air cells yet soft enough to spread; creaming works only inside this window, while too-warm fat melts and too-cold fat shatters instead of aerating.

A gluten-development endpoint: a small piece of dough is stretched thin enough to pass light through without tearing, indicating the gluten network is elastic and extensible enough to trap fermentation gas.

A proof-readiness test: a floured finger presses ~1 cm into the dough; a slow, partial spring-back leaving a slight dent means ready, an immediate full spring-back means underproofed, and no spring-back or collapse means overproofed.

The rapid final rise in the first ~8-12 minutes of baking, driven by thermal gas expansion, water flashing to steam, and a last burst of yeast activity before yeast dies at 54-60°C and proteins begin to set.

The continued internal temperature rise (typically ~2-6°C, more in large dense loaves) after an item leaves the oven, because the hot outer mass keeps conducting heat inward; it is the reason many items are pulled below their final target.

The firming that happens as starch retrogrades and fat/egg proteins solidify during cooling; custards, cheesecakes, and cakes that look underset when hot reach final texture only after cooling, so hot appearance is a poor doneness cue.

Controlled crystallization of cocoa butter into the stable Form V crystal by melting, cooling with seed, and reworking to a working temperature (~31-32°C dark, ~29-30°C milk/white), yielding snap and gloss; skipping it gives dull, streaky, soft chocolate.

Gradually raising the temperature of eggs by whisking in small additions of a hot liquid before combining fully, so the proteins warm evenly and set into a smooth custard instead of scrambling into curds.

Large vertical holes or channels in quick breads and muffins caused by overmixing, which develops gluten and forms gas escape paths; distinct from an evenly open yeast crumb and from uniform toughness.

The progression of a beaten egg or cream foam: soft peaks (tips flop over), medium peaks (tips curl), and stiff peaks (tips stand straight); overbeaten foam past stiff turns grainy and dry and can no longer be folded without collapsing.

source_registry.description: heuristic prior estimates for culinary_technique_doneness work units in absence of supplied datasets
source_registry.citation_or_locator: heuristic prior; no external dataset supplied

nodes.definition: The governing stance of the KB: technique is chosen backward from the target crumb (creaming for a fine tender cake, foam for an airy sponge, cut-in for flaky layers, kneading for chewy bread) and doneness is measured against an explicit signal hierarchy rather than eyeballed. Two principles run through everything: mechanical structure is built during mixing and set by heat, and the single most reliable done signal is internal temperature, with visual color the least reliable. A home cook applying this framework always asks 'what crumb do I want, and what number confirms it is set?' before touching an ingredient.

excluded: the specific temperature numbers per product

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the definition of doneness dominance or the method-selection principle is restated

pros.claim: Framing method choice from the target crumb prevents applying an aeration method to a product that needs the opposite structure
pros.example: a cook who wants flaky biscuits will not cream the butter soft when the framework tells them cold cut-in fat is what makes layers

cons.claim: The measure-everything stance adds thermometer steps that feel like overkill for very forgiving bakes
cons.example: probing a batch of drop cookies that are reliably done by edge color wastes a step the framework nominally demands

failure_modes: picking a method by habit rather than by the crumb it produces, so the texture is wrong before baking starts
treating color or time as the primary done signal, which the rest of the KB explicitly demotes
acceptance_tests: the statement names method-from-crumb selection and asserts internal temperature as the dominant done signal
revisit_triggers: a product family is added whose doneness is not governed by internal temperature
the downstream diagnosis nodes reveal a signal the framework never ranked

nodes.definition: Map each mixing method to the crumb it produces and pick by desired texture. Creaming (fat + sugar beaten to aerate, ~18-21°C fat) yields a fine, tender, evenly risen cake; the muffin/two-bowl method (liquid fats stirred minimally into dry) yields a tender, slightly coarse quick bread; biscuit/cut-in (cold solid fat cut into flour) yields flaky, layered pastry; foam/sponge (whipped egg carrying the air) yields a light, springy, low-fat crumb. The decision rule: aeration source (fat vs egg vs chemical) and gluten tolerance (high for bread, near-zero for tender cake) determine the method, and the method then dictates fat temperature and mixing limits downstream.

included: the four core methods and their resulting crumbs
selection by aeration source and gluten tolerance

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a mixing method is added or its crumb outcome is re-characterized

pros.claim: Selecting by aeration source makes the fat-temperature and mixing-limit choices deterministic instead of guesswork
pros.example: choosing foam method for a chiffon immediately tells the cook the air comes from eggs, so overmixing flour is the risk to guard

cons.claim: Hybrid recipes blur the method boundaries, so a single-label choice can under-serve a batter that borrows from two methods
cons.example: a hot-milk sponge both whips eggs and adds warm melted butter, fitting neither pure foam nor pure creaming

failure_modes: choosing creaming for a product that needs egg-foam lightness, giving a dense result
defaulting to one familiar method regardless of the crumb the recipe actually needs
acceptance_tests: each of the four methods is paired with its characteristic crumb and a selection criterion
revisit_triggers: a new method (e.g., reverse creaming, blitz lamination) must be slotted into the map
a downstream failure traces to a method mismatch the selector should have caught

nodes.definition: Beat solid fat with sugar so the sharp sugar crystals cut air pockets into the fat, seeding the bubbles that chemical leavening later expands. It works only inside the fat plasticity window, ~18-21°C (about 65-70°F): warmer fat melts and its air cells collapse into a greasy batter, colder fat is too rigid to fold air in. Cream 3-5 minutes until the mass is pale and increased in volume, then add eggs gradually to keep the emulsion from breaking. This method builds a fine, uniform, tender crumb and is the backbone of butter cakes, pound cakes, and many cookies.

included: gradual egg addition to hold the emulsion
excluded: doneness temperature of the finished cake

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the plasticity window is refined for a different fat or ambient condition

pros.claim: Correctly creamed batter carries a dense population of fine bubbles that give an even, close, tender crumb no other method matches for butter cakes
pros.example: a pound cake creamed at 20°C rises evenly with a velvety crumb rather than a coarse, holey one

cons.claim: The method is unforgiving of fat temperature, so a few degrees too warm breaks the emulsion and the aeration is lost
cons.example: butter softened to 27°C in a warm kitchen creams to a soupy, separated mass that bakes greasy and flat

failure_modes: fat above ~24°C melts and air escapes, giving a dense greasy cake — distinguished from undercreaming because the batter looks shiny and loose rather than stiff and pale
eggs added too fast curdle the emulsion, producing a broken batter that bakes with a coarse crumb
acceptance_tests: the fat window 18-21°C is stated and the aeration mechanism is explained as air trapped around sugar crystals
revisit_triggers: a fat other than dairy butter (shortening, high-ratio) shifts the workable plasticity window
reverse-creaming is adopted and changes the aeration logic

nodes.definition: Combine wet ingredients (including melted or liquid fat) in one bowl and dry in another, then fold the wet into the dry only until no dry streaks remain — typically 10-15 gentle strokes. The defining rule is deliberate undermixing: because the fat is liquid, no aeration comes from it, so all leavening is chemical and the goal is to hydrate flour without developing gluten. Overmixing is the signature failure, developing gluten and creating tunnels and toughness. It produces a tender, slightly coarse crumb typical of muffins, pancakes, and quick breads.

excluded: the flaky layering of cut-in method

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the mixing-stroke limit or fat-state assumption is revised

pros.claim: Minimal mixing guarantees a tender crumb because the gluten network never develops enough to toughen
pros.example: muffins folded to just-combined bake domed and tender, while the same batter beaten smooth bakes tough and tunneled

cons.claim: The undermix rule leaves visible batter lumps that novices over-correct by stirring, defeating the method
cons.example: a cook smoothing out every lump develops gluten and gets peaked, tunneled muffins

failure_modes: overmixing develops gluten and traps gas channels, giving tunnels and toughness — distinguished from a dense underleavened muffin because tunneled muffins are tall and peaked, not squat
under-hydration from too few strokes leaves dry flour pockets that bake as chalky spots
acceptance_tests: the just-combined mixing limit is stated and overmixing is named as the tunneling cause
revisit_triggers: a recipe uses solid rather than liquid fat, moving it toward creaming behavior
tunneling recurs despite following the stroke count, implying another cause

nodes.definition: Cut cold solid fat (butter kept below ~10°C, ideally near freezing for the flakiest result) into flour until it is in pea-to-flake-sized pieces, then add cold liquid and mix just to a shaggy dough. The cold fat pieces stay discrete; in the oven they melt and their water flashes to steam, prying the dough into flaky sheets. Handling must be minimal and quick so body heat does not melt the fat prematurely. This yields the flaky, layered structure of biscuits, scones, and pie crust — a fundamentally different texture from the fine crumb of creaming.

included: keeping fat cold and in discrete pieces

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the cold-fat temperature ceiling or fat-piece target size is revised

pros.claim: Discrete cold fat pieces create steam pockets that produce distinct flaky layers impossible to get from softened fat
pros.example: pie dough with visible butter flecks bakes into shattering flakes, while warmed butter blends in and bakes dense and mealy

cons.claim: The cold-fast requirement fights warm kitchens and slow hands, so the window to work the dough is short
cons.example: in a 26°C kitchen the butter softens within a minute of handling and the flakiness collapses

failure_modes: fat warmed above ~15°C blends into the flour and bakes dense/mealy — distinguished from overworked dough because the crumb is short and crumbly rather than tough and chewy
overworking after liquid is added develops gluten and turns biscuits tough and tight
acceptance_tests: the cold-fat requirement and steam-driven flaking mechanism are both stated
revisit_triggers: a laminated-shortcut method is introduced that changes fat-piece sizing
a non-butter fat with a different melt point is specified

nodes.definition: Build structure and lift from air whipped into eggs rather than from fat. Whip whole eggs, yolks, or whites (often with sugar) to a defined stage: soft peaks (tips flop when the whisk lifts, ~voluminous but loose), medium peaks (tips curl over), and stiff peaks (tips stand straight and glossy). Whites take air best when free of fat and yolk and near room temperature; sugar added gradually stabilizes the foam. Overwhipping past stiff turns the foam grainy, dry, and clumpy and it can no longer hold or fold. The whipped foam is then folded together with flour and any fat, producing the light, springy, low-fat crumb of génoise, chiffon, and angel food.

included: foam stability factors (fat-free bowl, gradual sugar)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a whip stage definition or foam-stability factor is refined

pros.claim: Egg foam delivers dramatic lift with little or no added fat, giving the springy low-fat crumb no creamed batter can match
pros.example: angel food cake rises tall and cottony from whipped whites alone with zero fat

cons.claim: The foam is fragile and stage-sensitive, so a bowl trace of fat or one over-beat destroys the whole structure
cons.example: a speck of yolk in the whites prevents them from reaching stiff peaks at all

failure_modes: overwhipping past stiff peak gives a grainy, curdled foam that weeps and collapses — distinguished from underwhipped foam because underwhipped is loose and wet while overwhipped is dry and clumpy
fat contamination or too-early sugar prevents the foam from ever gaining volume
acceptance_tests: soft, medium, and stiff peak stages are named and the overwhip failure is described
revisit_triggers: a stabilizer (cream of tartar, meringue powder) is introduced that shifts the whip endpoints
whipping cream rather than egg is the foam source

nodes.definition: Combine a light aerated mass (whipped foam) with a heavier one (flour, melted fat, or a base) while losing as little air as possible. The technique is cut-and-turn: a flexible spatula slices straight down through the center, sweeps along the bottom, and lifts the bottom mixture up and over the top, rotating the bowl a quarter turn each stroke. Add the lighter mass to the heavier in two or three additions, sacrificing the first to lighten the base. Stirring, beating, or over-folding shears the bubbles and deflates the batter; stopping too early leaves flour streaks that bake as dense stripes.

included: adding light to heavy in stages

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the folding motion or staging guidance is revised for a new batter type

pros.claim: Correct folding keeps most of the whipped air intact so the sponge bakes tall and even
pros.example: a génoise folded in three additions with a spatula holds volume where the same batter stirred would sink flat

cons.claim: The gentle technique is slow and the endpoint is a judgment call between deflation and unmixed streaks
cons.example: a cook rushing the fold either beats out the air or leaves flour pockets that bake as gummy streaks

failure_modes: over-folding or stirring deflates the batter, giving a flat dense cake — distinguished from streaking because a deflated batter is uniform and thin while an under-folded one shows visible flour or foam patches
under-folding leaves dry flour or unincorporated foam that bakes as dense stripes
acceptance_tests: the cut-and-turn motion and the add-light-to-heavy-in-stages rule are both described
revisit_triggers: a very dense base (e.g., pastry cream) requires a modified lightening step
repeated flat sponges suggest the fold count needs adjustment

nodes.definition: Develop the gluten network in wheat doughs by hydrating flour and working it so glutenin and gliadin proteins link into an elastic, extensible film that traps fermentation gas. Kneading (by hand ~8-12 minutes, by mixer ~5-8 minutes) or timed rest-and-fold cycles reach the endpoint judged by the windowpane test: a stretched piece thins to translucency without tearing. Enough development gives chewy, well-risen bread with an open crumb; too little gives a dense, crumbly loaf that cannot hold gas; too much (mostly by machine) breaks the dough down into a slack, sticky mass. This is the opposite goal of the tender-crumb methods, where gluten is minimized.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the windowpane target or kneading time range is revised for a flour type

pros.claim: A windowpane-tested dough holds fermentation gas and yields an open, chewy crumb that under-kneaded dough cannot
pros.example: a lean baguette dough kneaded to windowpane traps CO2 for an open, irregular crumb

cons.claim: Over-development is possible by machine and produces a slack, gummy dough that no proofing recovers
cons.example: a dough run 20 minutes in a stand mixer goes shiny, slack, and tears into strings instead of a windowpane

failure_modes: under-kneading leaves a weak network that bakes dense and tears when shaped — distinguished from overproof because under-kneaded dough never reached windowpane, not merely over-fermented
machine over-kneading breaks gluten into a slack sticky mass that spreads instead of holding shape
acceptance_tests: the windowpane endpoint is defined and both under- and over-development outcomes are stated
revisit_triggers: a high-hydration or whole-grain dough needs a different development strategy
a no-knead time-based development method is adopted

nodes.definition: Build many alternating layers of dough and butter by enclosing a butter block in dough and repeatedly rolling and folding (e.g., three or four letter/book folds). The controlling variable is butter temperature: the butter must stay pliable but cool, roughly 13-16°C, so it stretches into continuous sheets without either shattering (too cold, below ~10°C, tears the layers) or melting into the dough (too warm, above ~18°C, merges the layers and leaks fat). Chill the dough between folds to relax gluten and re-firm the butter. In the oven the layered water flashes to steam and lifts the sheets, giving the flaky rise of croissants and puff pastry. It builds on developed but relaxed gluten so the dough can be rolled thin without tearing.

excluded: proof and bake temperatures of the finished pastry

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the butter plasticity window or fold count is revised

pros.claim: Keeping butter in the pliable-cool window yields continuous unbroken layers that puff into hundreds of flaky sheets
pros.example: croissant dough rolled with butter at ~14°C laminates cleanly for an open honeycomb interior

cons.claim: The narrow butter window plus mandatory chilling makes lamination slow and easy to ruin between the two failure modes
cons.example: butter that firms to 8°C between folds cracks and punches through the dough on the next roll

failure_modes: butter too cold (<10°C) shatters and tears the dough, breaking layer continuity — distinguished from too-warm failure because cold failure shows cracked butter shards while warm failure shows greasy merged dough
butter too warm (>18°C) melts into the dough and the layers merge, leaking fat and baking dense
acceptance_tests: the 13-16°C butter window is stated with the shatter-vs-melt failure modes on either side
revisit_triggers: a high-butterfat European butter shifts the workable temperature window
an ambient kitchen temperature repeatedly forces the butter out of range

nodes.definition: Yeast is a live organism with sharp thermal thresholds that differ by product form. Active dry yeast (ADY) must be rehydrated in warm liquid at 40-43°C (about 105-110°F) before use; liquid much hotter kills it and much cooler under-activates it. Instant (rapid-rise) yeast is added dry directly to the flour and needs no rehydration; what matters is the final dough temperature target of 24-27°C (about 75-80°F) for a healthy, controllable ferment. Above roughly 46°C yeast is stressed and activity falls off, and yeast dies in the 54-60°C band — which is also why oven spring ends. Getting the form-versus-temperature pairing wrong is a whole-batch failure, not a texture nuance.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a yeast strain or form with different thermal thresholds is added

pros.claim: Naming the exact bands makes yeast handling deterministic and turns a common whole-batch failure into a checklist step
pros.example: measuring rehydration water at 42°C rather than pouring hot tap water saves a dough that would otherwise never rise

cons.claim: The bands assume a thermometer and controlled water, which off-the-cuff bakers skip and then misjudge by feel
cons.example: 'warm to the touch' tap water can be 50°C and quietly stress the yeast

failure_modes: rehydrating ADY at 54-60°C kills it and the dough never rises — distinguished from an underproof because the bulk shows no rise at all rather than a partial one
adding ADY dry (treating it like instant) leaves undissolved granules and a sluggish, uneven rise
acceptance_tests: the four bands (rehydrate 40-43°C, dough target 24-27°C, stress ~46°C, death 54-60°C) are all stated with the ADY-vs-instant distinction
revisit_triggers: a sourdough or wild-yeast culture with different thermal optima is in scope
an osmotolerant or specialty yeast changes the workable bands

nodes.definition: Judge fermentation and final proof by measurable endpoints, not the clock. Bulk fermentation runs until the dough has roughly doubled (or grown a defined 50-75% for stronger structure), showing a domed, gassy, jiggly mass. Final proof is judged by the poke test: a floured finger pressed ~1 cm into the shaped dough should spring back slowly and only partway, leaving a slight dent. An immediate full spring-back means underproofed (bake it and it will burst and be dense); no spring-back or a sighing collapse means overproofed (it will spread and fall). Temperature sets the pace — warmer proofs faster but with less flavor — so volume fraction and the poke test, not minutes, define the endpoint.

included: the poke test for final proof

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the volume-fraction target or poke-test interpretation is revised

pros.claim: Endpoint-by-signal beats timing because the same recipe proofs at wildly different speeds by temperature
pros.example: a dough that needs 90 minutes at 21°C is ready in 45 at 27°C; the poke test catches both

cons.claim: The poke test is a learned tactile judgment that reads differently across hydrations and flours
cons.example: a slack high-hydration dough barely springs back even when perfectly proofed, misleading a novice

failure_modes: underproof (full immediate spring-back) bakes dense and bursts at a weak seam — distinguished from overproof because underproofed dough springs vigorously while overproofed sighs and stays dented
overproof (no spring-back, collapse) spreads flat and bakes with a sour, coarse, sunken crumb
acceptance_tests: the volume-fraction bulk endpoint and the poke-test proof endpoint (partial slow spring-back) are both defined
revisit_triggers: a retarded cold-proof or sourdough schedule changes the endpoint behavior
a dough hydration outside the usual range makes the poke test read differently

nodes.definition: Temper chocolate to lock cocoa butter into the stable Form V crystal so it sets with snap, gloss, and shelf stability. Melt fully (dark to ~45-50°C, milk/white a few degrees lower to avoid scorching), cool while introducing seed crystals from tempered chocolate, then bring to the working temperature: about 31-32°C for dark and about 29-30°C for milk and white. Held in this narrow window the good crystals dominate; overheating past ~34°C (dark) melts them out and the chocolate must be re-tempered, while a drop of water seizes it into a grainy paste. Untempered chocolate sets dull, streaky (bloom), and soft.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the working-temperature targets are refined for a specific couverture

pros.claim: Hitting the working-temperature window gives a glossy hard shell with a clean snap that untempered chocolate never achieves
pros.example: dark couverture worked at 31.5°C sets shiny and snaps cleanly for dipped confections

cons.claim: The window is only a degree or two wide and any water contact seizes the batch, so the process is finicky and easy to lose
cons.example: a single drop of steam condensate turns fluid tempered chocolate into a stiff grainy lump

failure_modes: overheating past ~34°C melts the stable crystals and the chocolate sets dull and streaky (bloom) — distinguished from seizing because bloomed chocolate is smooth-but-dull while seized chocolate is grainy and stiff
water contact seizes the chocolate into a thick paste that cannot be poured or coated
acceptance_tests: the dark ~31-32°C and milk/white ~29-30°C working targets are stated along with the seed method
revisit_triggers: a compound (non-cocoa-butter) coating that does not require tempering is used instead
an unusually high- or low-fat couverture shifts the working temperatures

nodes.definition: Warm eggs gradually so they thicken a custard smoothly instead of scrambling. Whisk a small stream of the hot liquid (scalded milk or cream) into the beaten eggs to raise their temperature slowly, then return the combined mixture to the heat. The custard is cooked to the setting range of 76-82°C (about 170-180°F): below that it stays runny, and above ~82-85°C the proteins over-coagulate and the custard curdles into visible curds. Constant stirring and gentle heat keep the temperature even; a thermometer or the nappe (coats-the-back-of-a-spoon) cue marks the endpoint. This is the same principle as chocolate tempering — controlled thermal staging — applied to protein.

included: gradual heat equalization by streaming hot liquid in
the 76-82°C set range and curdle ceiling
excluded: baked custard doneness in a water bath (covered under internal-temp targets)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the set range or curdle ceiling is refined for a stabilized custard

pros.claim: Streaming hot liquid into eggs before cooking prevents the shock that scrambles them, giving a silky custard
pros.example: crème anglaise tempered gradually and pulled at 80°C is pourable and smooth rather than lumpy

cons.claim: The set-to-curdle margin is only a few degrees and carryover can push a just-set custard over it after the heat is off
cons.example: a custard pulled at 82°C off a hot burner keeps rising and curdles from residual heat

failure_modes: adding hot liquid too fast scrambles the eggs into curds — distinguished from overcooking because the curds appear instantly on contact rather than developing gradually with rising temperature
cooking past ~82-85°C over-coagulates the proteins so the custard curdles and weeps
acceptance_tests: the gradual-streaming technique and the 76-82°C set range with the curdle ceiling are stated
revisit_triggers: a starch-stabilized pastry cream that tolerates a boil changes the temperature ceiling
an egg-substitute or ultra-pasteurized dairy shifts the coagulation behavior

nodes.definition: Rank the signals that indicate doneness in strict priority: internal temperature dominates because it directly reports the physical state of the crumb (starch gelatinized, proteins set, moisture driven off); then a clean or crumb-specific skewer/toothpick read; then touch and springback (the top springs back and no longer holds a dent); and color LAST, because crust color reflects surface sugars and oven quirks, not the interior. When signals disagree, temperature wins. Color is the most seductive and least reliable cue: a dark pan or a hot spot browns the outside long before the center is set, and a pale convection bake can be fully done while looking underbaked.

included: the ordered ranking temperature > skewer > touch > color
excluded: the specific temperature numbers per product

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the signal ranking or the tie-break rule is restated or reordered

pros.claim: An explicit ranking resolves the most common doneness argument — the cake looks done but the center is raw — in favor of the signal that reflects the interior
pros.example: a deep bundt reads golden at 25 minutes but is 82°C inside; the hierarchy says keep baking to temperature

cons.claim: Strict temperature-first guidance can feel wrong for items with no clean probe point where touch and color are the practical cues
cons.example: thin tuiles or macaron shells set by color and feel because a probe cannot read a 3 mm layer

failure_modes: judging by color and pulling a browned but 82°C cake gives a raw sunken center — distinguished from an overbaked-dry result because the wet-vs-dry skewer read differs (see the sunk-center diagnosis)
trusting a clock over any physical signal in an uncalibrated oven
acceptance_tests: the four signals are ranked with internal temperature first and color last, and the temperature-wins tie-break is stated
revisit_triggers: a product family with no usable internal-probe point is added
a new instrument (e.g., infrared surface reading) changes which cue is most reliable

nodes.definition: The dominant doneness signal, expressed as center-temperature targets by product family: lean bread (crusty, low fat/sugar) is done at 96-99°C; enriched breads (with butter, egg, sugar) finish lower, roughly 85-93°C, because fat and sugar soften set; butter and sponge cakes are done at 93-99°C; cheesecake is pulled with the center at 65-70°C (still jiggly, it sets on cooling); molten/lava-style cakes are pulled at a center of 71-77°C to keep a flowing core; and stirred/baked custards set at 76-82°C. Probe the geometric center, avoiding the pan bottom and any molten pocket. These numbers are the anchor every secondary cue is checked against.

included: center-temperature targets for lean bread, enriched bread, cakes, cheesecake, molten, custard
excluded: the ranking rationale (owned by the hierarchy)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a product-family target is added or an existing target is corrected

pros.claim: Per-family targets turn doneness into a single reading instead of a judgment call and explain why one temperature cannot serve all products
pros.example: 89°C is perfect for brioche but leaves a lean sourdough gummy, which the family-specific targets make explicit

cons.claim: Targets are center readings, so poor probe placement (hitting a pan wall or a molten pocket) gives a false number
cons.example: a probe touching the hot pan bottom reads 105°C while the crumb center is only 88°C

failure_modes: using a bread target for a cheesecake overbakes it and cracks it — distinguished from an underbaked cheesecake because an overbaked one is dry and cracked while an underbaked one is soupy at center
probing off-center gives a reading that passes a raw center or fails a done one
acceptance_tests: lean bread 96-99°C, enriched lower, cakes 93-99°C, cheesecake 65-70°C, molten 71-77°C, and custard 76-82°C are all stated as center targets
revisit_triggers: a new product family (e.g., steamed cake, confit-style baked good) needs its own target
a measured discrepancy shows a family target is off for a common recipe

nodes.definition: The subordinate doneness cues used to corroborate (never override) internal temperature. The skewer/toothpick: a clean skewer means a cake is set, but note the product — a fudgy brownie is done with moist crumbs clinging, while liquid batter means keep baking. Touch/springback: a done sponge springs back from a light press and no longer holds a dent, and a loaf sounds hollow when tapped on the base. Color, ranked last: golden edges pulling from the pan wall are a hint, not proof, because pan color, rack position, and oven hot spots all shift browning independent of interior doneness. Each cue is read in the context of its product and always deferred to the thermometer.

included: skewer read (clean vs moist-crumb by product)

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a secondary cue's product-specific interpretation is revised

pros.claim: Secondary cues give a fast, no-probe sanity check and catch a mis-read thermometer or bad probe placement
pros.example: a cake reading 95°C that still sinks under a finger flags a probe placed in a done edge rather than the raw center

cons.claim: Each cue is product-dependent and routinely misleads when applied to the wrong item
cons.example: waiting for a clean skewer in a molten cake bakes out the very liquid core the recipe wants

failure_modes: reading a moist-crumb brownie skewer as raw and overbaking it — distinguished from a genuinely raw skewer because raw batter is wet and glossy while a done brownie leaves soft crumbs
trusting hollow-tap on an enriched loaf, whose soft crust muffles the sound even when done
acceptance_tests: skewer, springback/hollow-tap, and color are each described as product-dependent and subordinate to temperature
revisit_triggers: a product where a secondary cue is the only practical signal is added
a cue is found to mislead systematically for a common recipe

nodes.definition: Oven spring is the rapid final expansion in roughly the first 8-12 minutes of baking. Three forces drive it: trapped fermentation gas and dissolved CO2 expand as they heat, dough water flashes to steam, and the yeast makes a last vigorous burst of activity before it is killed in the 54-60°C band. The rise stops as proteins coagulate (~60-70°C) and starch gelatinizes (~60-85°C), setting the crumb. A well-proofed, well-scored loaf with adequate oven heat and steam springs tall; an overproofed loaf has spent its gas and barely rises; opening the door early or a cold oven lets the structure set before it can lift. It is the payoff of correct fermentation and the input to a properly risen crumb.

included: the set temperatures that end the rise
conditions that help or kill spring

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the set-temperature ranges or the drivers of spring are refined

pros.claim: Understanding oven spring tells the baker to load a hot, steamy oven and not open the door, protecting the final rise
pros.example: steaming the first 10 minutes lets a scored boule bloom open rather than setting a tight crust too early

cons.claim: Oven spring cannot rescue a dough that arrives over- or underproofed, so it is a payoff stage, not a control point
cons.example: an overproofed loaf loaded into a perfect oven still barely lifts because its gas is spent

failure_modes: a cold or dry oven sets the crust before the dough lifts, giving a squat loaf — distinguished from an overproof squat loaf because the underspring loaf still poke-tests as underproofed while the overproof one had collapsed before baking
opening the door during the spring window drops the temperature and stalls the rise
acceptance_tests: the three drivers (gas expansion, steam, final yeast burst) and the set temperatures ending the rise are stated
revisit_triggers: a steam-injection or Dutch-oven method changes the spring dynamics
a batter leavened chemically rather than by yeast needs a separate rise model

nodes.definition: Account for what happens after the item leaves the oven. Carryover cooking: the hot outer mass keeps conducting heat inward, so the center rises another ~2-6°C (more in large dense loaves, negligible in thin cookies) — which is why custards and delicate cakes are pulled a few degrees below their final target so they land on it rather than overshoot. Cool-set: starch retrogrades and egg/fat proteins firm as the item cools, so cheesecakes and custards that look loose when hot reach their real texture only after chilling. The rule is to pull at target-minus-carryover and to judge final set after cooling, never by hot appearance.

included: the ~2-6°C carryover rise and its dependence on mass
cool-set firming of starch and protein

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the carryover range or cool-set behavior is refined for a format

pros.claim: Pulling at target-minus-carryover prevents the systematic overbake that comes from waiting until the probe reads the final number in the oven
pros.example: pulling a custard at 79°C so carryover carries it to ~82°C gives a set-but-silky result instead of curdled

cons.claim: Carryover magnitude varies with mass and pan, so a single subtract-a-number rule misfires across item sizes
cons.example: the 5°C margin that suits a large loaf overshoots a small ramekin custard that barely carries over

failure_modes: ignoring carryover and baking to the final number in-oven overshoots and dries or curdles the item — distinguished from a truly underbaked result because a carryover-overshot item was at target when pulled, not below it
judging cool-set items by hot appearance and re-baking a cheesecake that would have set on chilling
acceptance_tests: the ~2-6°C carryover rise and the cool-set firming are both stated with the pull-early rule
revisit_triggers: a very large or very thin format changes the carryover magnitude materially
a new setting mechanism (gelatin, starch) alters cool-set behavior

nodes.definition: A sunk center has two opposite causes with opposite fixes, told apart by the skewer. A WET-skewer sink (gummy, damp crumb, dense band at the bottom) means underbaked: the structure never set before the rise could be supported — fix by baking longer, often at a slightly lower temperature for more even heat, and confirm the center reaches its internal-temperature target. A DRY-crater sink (fully baked, dry crumb, cratered or fallen top) means the opposite: over-leavening, overproofing, too much sugar/fat weakening the structure, or opening the oven during the rise — fix by reducing leavener, cutting the proof, or leaving the door shut. Applying the underbake fix (more time) to a dry-crater failure only worsens it, which is why the skewer read must come first.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a new sunk-center signature or fix is identified

pros.claim: The wet-vs-dry differential prevents the single most damaging mistake — treating an over-leavened crater as underbaked and baking it even drier
pros.example: a fallen cake with a dry crater gets its leavener cut next time, not more oven minutes that would scorch it

cons.claim: Mixed causes can produce an ambiguous skewer (a large cake underbaked in the center yet over-leavened) that the clean binary does not resolve
cons.example: a tall cake both sank from excess baking powder and stayed wet in the middle, showing signals of both

failure_modes: misreading a dry-crater sink as underbaked and adding time, drying the crumb further — the differential is the wet vs dry skewer read at the sunken center
assuming every sink is under-leavening and cutting rise when the real cause was underbaking
acceptance_tests: the wet-skewer (underbake, bake longer) and dry-crater (over-leaven/overproof, reduce) causes are stated as having opposite fixes
revisit_triggers: a recipe class shows a third distinct sink signature not covered by wet vs dry
the internal-temperature target for the product is revised and changes the underbake threshold

nodes.definition: A dense, heavy crumb has three separable causes distinguished by what the batter or dough did earlier. Dead leavening (yeast killed by hot water, or stale/expired baking powder/soda) shows no rise at all — the bulk or batter never grew; fix by verifying leavener viability and yeast water temperature. Deflation shows a batter that rose and then fell — over-folding, overmixing an aerated batter, or knocking out gas after proof; fix by gentler handling and folding technique. Underproof/under-development shows a dough that rose only partway and poke-tests with a full spring-back; fix by proofing to endpoint or developing gluten to windowpane. The tell is the history: never rose (dead), rose then fell (deflated), or rose only partway (underproofed).

included: the dead-leavening vs deflation vs underproof differential

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a dense-crumb cause or its rise-history tell is revised

pros.claim: Separating the three causes by rise history stops the common error of adding leavener when the real fault was deflation from overmixing
pros.example: a cook who over-folded a sponge learns to fold gently rather than doubling the baking powder

cons.claim: Rise history is often unobserved after the fact, so diagnosis from the baked crumb alone is less certain
cons.example: given only a dense finished muffin, dead soda and overmixing can look similar without knowing whether it rose

failure_modes: treating a deflation-dense crumb as under-leavened and adding more leavener, which over-leavens the next batch — the differential is whether the batter rose then fell versus never rose
blaming the oven for density when the leavener was simply dead
acceptance_tests: the three causes (dead leavening, deflation, underproof) are separated by rise history with distinct fixes
revisit_triggers: a chemically and biologically leavened hybrid needs a combined viability check
a new dense-crumb cause appears that the three-way split does not cover

nodes.definition: Toughness and tunneling both come from too much gluten development in a product that wanted little, but they present differently. A tough crumb is uniformly chewy, tight, and rubbery throughout — the whole batter or dough was overmixed or over-kneaded for its type (a cake mixed like bread). Tunneling is localized: large vertical holes or channels run through an otherwise ordinary quick-bread or muffin crumb, formed when overmixing develops gluten strands that trap escaping gas into channels, often paired with a peaked rather than domed top. Fix both by mixing less: the muffin/two-bowl method's just-combined limit for quick breads, and matching kneading to the target (full windowpane for bread, none for tender cake). The differential is uniform chew (tough) versus visible vertical channels with a peak (tunneling).

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: the tough-vs-tunneling differential or fix is revised

pros.claim: Distinguishing uniform toughness from tunneling pins the fix to the exact mixing step that went too far
pros.example: peaked, tunneled muffins point straight to overmixing the two-bowl batter, not to the leavener or oven

cons.claim: The two can co-occur and mild tunneling is easy to miss on a cut that avoids a channel
cons.example: a muffin sliced off-center hides its tunnels and looks merely a bit tough

failure_modes: reading tough uniform chew as under-leavening and adding leavener, when the fix was to mix less — the differential is uniform density (overmixing/toughness) versus large vertical channels with a peaked top (tunneling)
attributing tunnels to oven temperature rather than to gluten developed during mixing
acceptance_tests: overmixing is named as the shared cause and the uniform-chew vs vertical-channel differential with the mix-less fix is stated
revisit_triggers: a batter with intentional gluten (e.g., popovers) needs a separate reading of channels
a gluten-free formulation removes the overmixing cause and needs its own diagnosis

nodes.definition: Once a defect is diagnosed, decide whether this bake can be salvaged or whether the fix is only for next time. A useful rule: thermal and set defects are often recoverable in-process (an underbaked but not-yet-collapsed cake can go back in the oven; a barely-under-tempered chocolate can be re-seeded; a runny custard can be gently brought up a few more degrees), but structural and leavening defects are usually terminal for the current item (a fallen over-proofed loaf, a deflated sponge, an overmixed-tough crumb, curdled custard) and only preventable next time by fixing proof, mixing, or leavener. The decision hinges on whether the structure is still intact: if the network can still hold, recover; if it has already collapsed or set wrong, accept the loss and change the upstream step. Recording which defects are recoverable saves the reflex of ruining a salvageable item or wasting effort on a doomed one.

probabilistic_layer.update_signal: a defect's recoverable-vs-terminal classification changes

pros.claim: Classifying defects as recoverable or terminal stops both wasted rescue effort and the loss of items that could have been saved
pros.example: an underbaked-but-standing cake goes back in the oven rather than being tossed, while a collapsed loaf is written off with a proof fix noted

cons.claim: The intact-structure test is a judgment that can misclassify a marginal item, leading to a failed rescue
cons.example: a cake right at the edge of collapse is returned to the oven and finishes sunken anyway

failure_modes: attempting to rescue a structurally collapsed item (fallen loaf, deflated sponge) wastes time and rarely works — distinguished from a recoverable defect because the structure has already fallen rather than merely being under-set
discarding a salvageable underbaked item that only needed more oven time
acceptance_tests: the recoverable-vs-terminal split is stated with the structure-intact decision rule and a prevention log
revisit_triggers: a defect currently marked terminal proves recoverable with a new technique
the diagnostic nodes add a defect that needs a recovery classification

edges.why_related: method selection operationalizes the framework's method-from-crumb principle
creaming is one of the methods the selector chooses among
the two-bowl method is a selectable option for tender quick breads
cut-in is the method chosen when flaky layers are the target crumb
foam/sponge is chosen when the air comes from egg rather than fat
folding is the step that combines the whipped foam without losing its air
kneading is the high-gluten path the selector chooses for chewy breads
lamination needs a developed-but-relaxed gluten dough to roll thin without tearing
the framework's thermal-control principle is instantiated by the yeast bands
healthy yeast within its bands is the precondition for a proof that reaches its endpoint
a developed gluten network is what traps the gas the proof endpoint measures
chocolate tempering is a thermal-control technique the framework governs
egg tempering is a thermal-staging technique the framework governs
the hierarchy makes the framework's measure-don't-guess doneness stance concrete
the temperature targets supply the numbers the hierarchy ranks first
the secondary cues are the lower-ranked signals the hierarchy subordinates to temperature
oven spring is the payoff of a correctly reached proof endpoint
carryover and cool-set adjust when to pull relative to the target temperature
diagnosing a sink relies on reading signals in the hierarchy's order
confirming an underbaked wet-skewer sink requires the center temperature target
diagnosing deflation requires knowing the method's intended aeration
the underproof cause of dense crumb is read against the proof endpoint
tunneling is the signature failure of overmixing the two-bowl method
toughness is over-application of gluten development to a tender product
the recovery decision consumes the sunk-center differential to classify the defect
the recovery decision consumes the dense-crumb differential to classify the defect
the recovery decision consumes the tough/tunneling differential to classify the defect
both are aeration methods, but creaming traps air in fat while foam traps it in egg, driving different fat-temperature and mixing constraints
the yeast's last vigorous burst before dying at 54-60°C is one of the forces that produces oven spring
kneading maximizes gluten and agitation while folding minimizes both to protect air, so the two techniques pull in opposite directions
edges.resolution_rule: choose by target crumb: develop gluten to windowpane for chewy bread, fold gently for foam/sponge cakes; never knead an aerated batter

edges.why_related: a dry-crater collapse traced to overproofing feeds back to tighten the proof endpoint on the next attempt
both are 'tempering' — controlled thermal staging to a narrow target window — one crystallizing cocoa butter, the other coagulating egg protein without shocking it
a tempered custard must still be brought to the 76-82°C set window, so the tempering technique and the doneness target jointly constrain the cook
both hinge on fat plasticity but at different windows — creaming needs pliable 18-21°C butter to aerate, lamination needs cooler 13-16°C butter to sheet without merging
both are minimal-mixing quick methods that avoid gluten, differing in fat state — liquid fat stirred in versus cold solid fat cut in

conflict_axes.name: temperature versus color for doneness
conflict_axes.description: Whether to trust the internal-temperature reading or the crust color when the two disagree about whether an item is done.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: internal temperature dominates; color is a last-rank corroborating hint because pan, rack, and hot spots brown the surface independent of interior set

conflict_axes.name: aeration versus tenderness
conflict_axes.description: Whether to mix enough to aerate and build structure or to minimize mixing to protect a tender crumb.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: let the target crumb decide: aerate by the method's mechanism (creaming, whipping) but stop before gluten develops in tender products

conflict_axes.name: warm plastic fat versus cold firm fat
conflict_axes.description: Whether fat should be pliable-warm to aerate or cold to create flaky layers.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: creaming needs the 18-21°C plasticity window; cut-in and lamination need cold discrete fat for steam-driven flaking — the method dictates the temperature

conflict_axes.name: underproof versus overproof
conflict_axes.description: The tension between proofing too little (dense, bursting) and too much (collapsed, sour, no spring).
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: use the poke test: partial slow spring-back is the endpoint; full spring-back means keep going, no spring-back means it is past

conflict_axes.name: pull early versus bake to number in oven
conflict_axes.description: Whether to pull below target and rely on carryover or bake until the probe reads the final target in the oven.
poles: bake until core hits target in-oven
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: for dense or delicate items pull early so carryover lands on target; for thin low-mass items with little carryover bake closer to the number

conflict_axes.name: instrument precision versus tactile speed
conflict_axes.description: Whether to probe with a thermometer every bake or rely on touch, springback, and experience for speed.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: probe whenever an item has a usable center and the stakes of error are high; reserve pure touch judgment for thin items no probe can read

conflict_axes.name: fast warm ferment versus slow cool ferment
conflict_axes.description: Whether to proof warm for speed or cool for flavor and control, given yeast's thermal sensitivity.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: keep dough within the 24-27°C target for control; go cooler and longer for flavor, never so warm as to approach the 46°C stress band

conflict_axes.name: gluten development versus tenderness
conflict_axes.description: Whether to work the dough to a strong gluten network or stop at just-combined to keep the crumb tender.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: match development to the product: full windowpane for chewy bread, near-zero for cakes and quick breads; folding preserves rather than builds

conflict_axes.name: recovery versus prevention
conflict_axes.description: Whether to try to salvage the current bake or accept the loss and fix the upstream step next time.
conflict_axes.resolution_hint: recover thermal/set defects while structure is intact; treat collapsed structural and leavening defects as terminal and log the upstream fix

edge_cases.description: High-altitude baking shifts proof pace, oven spring, and set temperatures
edge_cases.trigger: baking above roughly 1000 m where lower air pressure speeds gas expansion and lowers water's boiling point
edge_cases.mitigation: shorten proof, reduce leavener, and expect lean-bread doneness near the locally lowered boiling point rather than the sea-level 96-99°C

edge_cases.description: Dark or convection oven browns the crust before the center is set
edge_cases.trigger: using a dark metal pan or a fan oven that accelerates surface browning
edge_cases.mitigation: ignore the early color, probe the center to its temperature target, and tent with foil if the surface darkens before the interior is done

edge_cases.description: ADY versus instant yeast handling is confused
edge_cases.trigger: dissolving instant yeast in 40-43°C water or adding active dry yeast straight into the flour
edge_cases.mitigation: confirm the yeast form first; rehydrate only ADY at 40-43°C and add instant dry with a 24-27°C dough target

edge_cases.description: Cheesecake looks wet at its correct pull temperature
edge_cases.trigger: judging a cheesecake by surface jiggle instead of a 65-70°C center reading
edge_cases.mitigation: pull at 65-70°C center while the middle still jiggles and let cool-set finish it; baking to a firm hot center cracks and dries it

edge_cases.description: Molten/lava cake needs an intentionally unset core
edge_cases.trigger: applying a normal cake doneness cue (clean skewer, full set) to a molten dessert
edge_cases.mitigation: pull with the center at 71-77°C so the core stays flowing; a clean skewer means it is already overbaked

edge_cases.description: Custard curdles from carryover after leaving the heat
edge_cases.trigger: pulling a stirred custard at the top of its range on a hot pan so residual heat pushes it past ~82-85°C
edge_cases.mitigation: pull a few degrees early (around 79°C), remove from the hot pan, and stir over an ice bath to stop the rise

edge_cases.description: Slack high-hydration or sourdough dough reads the poke test differently
edge_cases.trigger: applying the standard poke test to a very wet or wild-yeast dough that barely springs back
edge_cases.mitigation: calibrate the poke expectation to the dough's slackness and combine with the volume-fraction cue rather than spring-back alone

edge_cases.description: Egg foam is beaten past stiff peak
edge_cases.trigger: over-whipping whites or whole eggs until they turn grainy and dry
edge_cases.mitigation: stop at the stage the recipe needs; a broken foam cannot be folded, so re-whip fresh whites rather than trying to save it

edge_cases.trigger: a drop of water reaching the bowl or overheating dark chocolate past ~34°C
edge_cases.mitigation: keep all water away and hold the working window; if it loses temper, re-melt and re-seed rather than pouring it out of range

edge_cases.description: Opening the oven during oven spring collapses a delicate rise
edge_cases.trigger: opening the door in the first 8-12 minutes of a soufflé, sponge, or lean loaf
edge_cases.mitigation: leave the door shut through the spring window and rely on the oven light, then probe only once a crust or set has formed

edge_cases.description: Low-protein or gluten-free batter gives a false wet-skewer read
edge_cases.trigger: probing a gluten-free or very moist batter that reads gummy on the skewer even when set
edge_cases.mitigation: defer to the internal-temperature target rather than the skewer, since these batters stay tacky at the center even when done

workflow.action: select the mixing method from the target crumb
workflow.description: decide creaming, two-bowl, cut-in, foam, or kneading based on the desired texture and aeration source
workflow.artifact: a chosen method with its implied fat-temperature and mixing-limit rules
workflow.gate: the method matches the target crumb and its constraints are noted

workflow.action: condition fat and eggs to the method's temperature
workflow.description: bring butter to the 18-21°C plasticity window for creaming, or keep it cold for cut-in and lamination, and eggs to the state the method needs
workflow.gate: a thermometer or feel confirms the fat is in the right window for the method

workflow.action: mix or develop to the method's endpoint
workflow.description: knead bread to windowpane, whip egg foam to the target peak, or stop a two-bowl batter at just-combined
workflow.artifact: a batter or dough at its correct development endpoint
workflow.gate: the endpoint test (windowpane, peak stage, or no dry streaks) passes

workflow.description: combine whipped foam with base and flour by cut-and-turn in stages to preserve air
workflow.gate: no flour streaks remain and the batter has not visibly deflated

workflow.description: bulk ferment to the volume fraction and final-proof to a partial slow poke-test spring-back
workflow.artifact: a proofed dough at its endpoint
workflow.gate: the poke test shows partial slow spring-back, not full spring-back or collapse

workflow.action: load a hot oven and protect the oven-spring window
workflow.description: bake in a preheated (and for lean bread, steamy) oven and keep the door shut through the first 8-12 minutes
workflow.artifact: an item that has completed its rise and begun to set
workflow.gate: the door stayed shut during the spring window and the item rose before setting

workflow.action: probe the center to its internal-temperature target
workflow.description: insert a calibrated probe at the geometric center and compare against the product family's target
workflow.gate: the center reading meets the product's target band

workflow.description: confirm with a product-appropriate skewer, springback, and color read, deferring to the thermometer on any disagreement
workflow.gate: secondary cues agree with the temperature or the discrepancy is explained by probe placement

workflow.action: pull with carryover margin and let it cool-set
workflow.description: pull at target-minus-carryover for dense or delicate items and judge final texture only after cooling
workflow.gate: the item landed on target after carryover and set correctly on cooling

workflow.action: if defective, run the differential diagnosis and classify recovery versus prevention
workflow.description: read the defect's distinguishing signals, decide whether the structure is still intact enough to salvage, and log the upstream fix
workflow.artifact: a diagnosis with a recover-or-prevent decision and a logged fix
workflow.gate: the defect is correctly differentiated and the recover-or-prevent decision follows the structure-intact rule

priority_rationale: The framework and method selection come first because every downstream technique and doneness call depends on choosing the right method and adopting the measure-don't-guess stance; the mixing, thermal-control, and proof nodes build on that, the doneness hierarchy and temperature targets anchor judgment, and the failure-diagnosis nodes sit last because they consume all the earlier signals to differentiate lookalike defects.

dominance_rules.rationale: color reflects surface sugars and oven quirks, not the interior state
dominance_rules.trigger: a browned surface disagrees with a below-target center reading
dominance_rules.action: keep baking to the center temperature target and tent the surface if it over-browns

dominance_rules.rationale: oven calibration, pan, and load make clock times unreliable
dominance_rules.trigger: the recipe time has elapsed but the center is below target
dominance_rules.action: trust the probe and continue baking to target

dominance_rules.rule: the poke test beats the clock for proof
dominance_rules.rationale: proof pace varies sharply with temperature and dough strength
dominance_rules.trigger: a scheduled proof time is reached but the poke test disagrees
dominance_rules.action: proof to the partial-slow-spring-back endpoint regardless of the clock

dominance_rules.rule: fat temperature beats recipe timing for creaming
dominance_rules.rationale: outside the 18-21°C window the aeration fails no matter how long you beat
dominance_rules.trigger: butter is warmer or colder than the plasticity window
dominance_rules.action: adjust the fat to the window before creaming rather than beating longer

dominance_rules.rule: the wet-versus-dry skewer read beats a generic 'bake it longer'
dominance_rules.rationale: underbake and over-leavening produce lookalike sinks with opposite fixes
dominance_rules.trigger: a cake has sunk in the center
dominance_rules.action: read the skewer first; add oven time only for a wet-skewer underbake, never for a dry-crater collapse

dominance_rules.rule: carryover margin beats baking to the exact number in-oven for delicate items
dominance_rules.rationale: residual heat keeps raising the center after removal
dominance_rules.trigger: a custard or delicate cake nears its target on a hot pan or in a hot oven
dominance_rules.action: pull at target-minus-carryover so it lands on target rather than overshooting

dominance_rules.rule: the windowpane test beats a fixed knead time
dominance_rules.rationale: development rate depends on flour, hydration, and method
dominance_rules.trigger: a knead-time minute count is reached
dominance_rules.action: knead to the windowpane endpoint rather than stopping on the clock

dominance_rules.rationale: if the leavening is dead, no additional time will produce a rise
dominance_rules.trigger: a dough or batter shows no rise at all
dominance_rules.action: verify yeast viability and leavener freshness before allowing more proof time

dominance_rules.rule: the product-specific temperature target beats a single universal doneness number
dominance_rules.rationale: cheesecake, molten cake, custard, and lean bread set at very different centers
dominance_rules.trigger: one is tempted to apply a familiar doneness temperature to a different product family
dominance_rules.action: use the family-specific target (e.g., 65-70°C cheesecake, 96-99°C lean bread), not a one-size number

anti_rework_rules.rule: verify yeast viability and water temperature before mixing
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a whole batch that never rises because the yeast was dead or killed

anti_rework_rules.rule: bring fat to the 18-21°C window before creaming
anti_rework_rules.prevents: a broken, greasy batter that must be discarded and re-made

anti_rework_rules.rule: calibrate and insert the thermometer before assuming an item is done
anti_rework_rules.prevents: under- or over-baked items pulled on color or time

anti_rework_rules.rule: run the poke test before committing the loaf to the oven
anti_rework_rules.prevents: an under- or over-proofed bake that bursts or collapses

anti_rework_rules.rule: confirm the yeast form before hydrating it
anti_rework_rules.prevents: killing instant yeast in hot water or leaving ADY undissolved

anti_rework_rules.rule: chill laminating butter to the 13-16°C window before rolling
anti_rework_rules.prevents: butter shattering or melting through the dough and forcing a re-laminate

anti_rework_rules.rule: fold rather than stir aerated batters
anti_rework_rules.prevents: deflated batter that bakes flat and must be re-whipped from scratch

anti_rework_rules.rule: differentiate the defect (wet-skewer versus dry-crater, tough versus tunneled) before adjusting the recipe
anti_rework_rules.prevents: applying the opposite fix and reproducing or worsening the failure
curdled custards and dried cakes from overshooting the target after removal

iteration_protocol.trigger: a cake or loaf sank in the center
iteration_protocol.action: read the skewer to separate wet-underbake from dry-crater over-leavening and apply the matching (opposite) fix

iteration_protocol.trigger: the crumb came out dense and heavy
iteration_protocol.action: classify by rise history as dead leavening, deflation, or underproof and fix the identified cause

iteration_protocol.trigger: the crumb is tough or shows tunnels
iteration_protocol.action: reduce mixing to the method's limit and match gluten development to the product

iteration_protocol.trigger: the thermometer disagrees with color or a skewer
iteration_protocol.action: trust the internal temperature, recalibrate expectations for the pan and oven, and tent if browning early

iteration_protocol.trigger: the poke test is ambiguous or the proof timing is off
iteration_protocol.action: recalibrate the endpoint to the dough's hydration and adjust proof temperature or time

iteration_protocol.trigger: chocolate set dull, streaky, or soft
iteration_protocol.action: re-melt and re-temper by seeding back into the working window

iteration_protocol.trigger: moving to a new oven, altitude, or product format
iteration_protocol.action: re-verify the internal-temperature targets and the carryover margin before trusting old cues
